Each system–dataset combination has only two synchronous and three asynchronous sessions, yet Tables 1–2 report numerous unpaired t-tests without identifying their observational units or accounting for repeated participants and dependent theme comparisons. Important reporting gaps remain despite the useful supplementary material: participant-to-session allocation, session durations, the exact SBERT checkpoint, LLM decoding settings, and the interview sample size and analysis procedure are unclear. strengths: The paper addresses a relevant NLP evaluation problem: how collaborative workflows affect interactive qualitative coding. Comparing three methodological families across two contrasting corpora provides useful breadth.

The evaluation combines several complementary diagnostics with a substantial human audit of 2,400 document–theme assignments. Double annotation, adjudication, and reported agreement provide valuable evidence beyond embedding similarities.
The presentation is generally clear. Final theme inventories, prompt templates, implementation details, and a public code/data link support inspection and potential reuse.
weaknesses: The design does not isolate collaboration modality (§4). Three-person synchronous teams are compared with individual coders, without the asynchronous consolidation described in the introduction. Human effort and participant expertise are not adequately controlled or reported, and returning participants always complete asynchronous coding first. Group size, experience, and order effects therefore offer alternative explanations for the observed differences.

The significance analysis does not establish reliable collaboration effects. Each system–dataset combination has only two synchronous codebooks and three asynchronous codebooks, yet Tables 1–2 report unpaired t-tests without identifying the sampling unit, sample sizes, or degrees of freedom. Themes, document pairs, and comparisons sharing codebooks are dependent; treating them as independent would inflate significance. Dependence-aware uncertainty and multiplicity handling are needed. Describing Climate improvements of 0.01 for the relational and LLM systems as uniformly 'much more cohesive' also overstates their demonstrated magnitude.

Experimental accounting needs reconciliation. The stated design requires 36 synchronous coder participations, but §4.2 reports 33 participants who each undertake at most one synchronous experiment. Moreover, Tables 15–16 list identical theme sets for corresponding relational and LLM Climate sessions without explaining their reuse. A participant/session mapping and explicit account of shared codebooks are necessary to determine the independent evidence supporting cross-system conclusions.

The central human-evaluation metric is insufficiently specified. Figure 4 reports F1, whereas §5.3 describes judging whether sampled assigned document–theme pairs are correct. This does not explain how false negatives or reference labels are obtained, which averaging scheme is used, or how sampling and unassigned documents affect the score. The annotation rubric, metric computation, coverage treatment, and uncertainty must be specified before the correctness comparisons are reproducible.

The proposed metrics are useful diagnostics, but their interpretation as qualitative-analysis quality needs validation. Maximum matching permits many-to-one alignments and depends on theme granularity, which varies substantially across sessions. Selecting the closest 25% of documents using embeddings also favors cohesion measured in that same space. These results do not by themselves demonstrate deeper analysis or better codebooks; sensitivity analyses and human judgments of thematic quality would strengthen that claim.

Several broader conclusions exceed the evidence. Two corpora differing simultaneously in topic, genre, size, and length cannot establish independent effects of particular dataset characteristics. One 3B model and its selected prompting workflow provide limited support for general claims about LLM reliability and cost. The interview findings also lack participant counts and a documented analysis procedure. The paper could support a useful exploratory contribution, but the experimental accounting, statistical analysis, and correctness measurement require important revisions before it meets the soundness and reproducibility threshold for Findings.

strengths: The paper addresses a relevant question for human-in-the-loop NLP: how collaboration settings affect qualitative coding outcomes. Its contribution is an empirical evaluation of practical workflows, with clear relevance to computational social science.

Comparing three substantially different systems across two contrasting corpora provides useful breadth. Separating consistency, cohesiveness, distinctiveness, and assignment correctness recognizes that coding quality has multiple dimensions.

The manual audit of 2,400 document-theme pairs provides valuable human evidence. Double annotation, adjudication, and reported Krippendorff’s alpha values of 0.632 and 0.696 make annotation reliability assessable.

The manuscript is generally well organized. Theme inventories, prompt templates, initialization details, computational information, and a public repository link provide useful support for transparency and reproduction.
weaknesses: The central comparison does not isolate collaboration timing. Asynchronous participants code individually without a consolidation stage, whereas synchronous conditions use three-person teams. Team size, available human effort, and collaboration are therefore entangled. Repeated participants also always complete the asynchronous experiment first, introducing potential learning effects. The results support an exploratory comparison of individual and group workflows; stronger conclusions about synchronous versus asynchronous collaboration require additional controls or explicit reframing.

The statistical evidence is insufficiently specified for the central significance claims. Each system/dataset has only two synchronous and three asynchronous codebooks, yet Tables 1–2 report unpaired t-tests without identifying the sampling unit or accounting for dependence among themes, shared codebook comparisons, and repeated participants. Treating themes or document pairs as independent would not establish general effects across coding sessions. Session-level uncertainty, effect sizes, and handling of multiple comparisons are needed. The 'near statistically significant' annotations should not strengthen the conclusions.

The experimental accounting needs reconciliation. The stated design requires 36 synchronous participant slots, but Section 4.2 reports 33 participants and at most one synchronous experiment per participant. Furthermore, Tables 15–16 contain the same Climate theme inventories for corresponding relational and LLM sessions. This may reflect intentional reuse, but its extent and implications are unexplained. A participant-to-session map and an explicit account of independently elicited versus reused material are necessary to assess the evidence.

The correctness metric is not reproducible from its description. Figure 4 reports F1, while Section 5.3 describes checking sampled predicted document-theme assignments; it does not explain how false negatives, recall, or averaging are defined. Sampling weights, uncertainty, and treatment of unmapped or invalid-label documents are also unclear, despite Table 4 reporting invalid labels for up to 16.1% of a dataset. These omissions materially affect comparisons between systems with different coverage.

Maximum theme matching permits many-to-one alignments and is sensitive to theme granularity, which varies substantially across sessions. Human theme-alignment judgments or suitable size-matched baselines would help establish whether these scores support claims of clearer themes and deeper analysis.

Two corpora differing simultaneously in size, genre, topic, length, and repetition cannot establish independent effects of particular dataset characteristics. Likewise, one Llama 3.2 3B configuration does not support broad conclusions about LLM cost and reliability. The interview synthesis omits its sample size and analysis procedure. strengths: Addresses a relevant evaluation problem for NLP-assisted qualitative analysis: how collaboration settings interact with tools and datasets. The contribution has value as an empirical study without requiring a new modeling method.

Examines three distinct approaches across two corpora and 30 reported coding sessions. Separating consistency, cohesiveness, distinctiveness, and assignment correctness helps expose trade-offs that a single metric would obscure.

Includes substantial human evaluation: 2,400 document–theme pairs, two annotators per assignment, adjudication, and reported Krippendorff’s alpha values of 0.632 and 0.696. This provides useful evidence beyond embedding-based measurements.

The manuscript is generally understandable and provides extensive theme lists, prompt templates, corpus analyses, and a public code/data link. Holding initial partitions fixed within systems also improves comparability.
weaknesses: The central collaboration-effect claim is not established by the design. Section 4 compares three-person joint codebooks with individual codebooks, without a documented asynchronous consolidation step. Collaboration timing therefore changes alongside team size and aggregation of perspectives. Returning participants always completed asynchronous coding first, introducing possible learning effects. Allocation and time budgets are insufficiently documented. These observations need a narrower interpretation or a controlled replication.

The statistical analysis is insufficiently specified for the main conclusions. Each system–dataset combination has only two synchronous and three asynchronous codebooks, yet Tables 1–2 report numerous significant differences without identifying the test observations, sample sizes, or dependence handling. Treating themes or document pairs as independent replicates would constitute pseudoreplication. Session-level uncertainty, participant reuse, and multiple comparisons need attention. Changes such as 0.44 versus 0.43 in Climate relational cohesiveness particularly require transparent analysis.

The proposed quality measures lack sufficient validation. Maximum matching permits many-to-one alignments and is sensitive to theme granularity. LLM centroid similarities of approximately 0.94–0.98 coexist with Jaccard scores of 0.09–0.17, making their interpretation uncertain without baselines or expert validation. Selecting documents nearest centroids and evaluating them in the same embedding space also favors higher cohesiveness by construction; it does not independently establish clearer or more useful themes.

The correctness evaluation is underdefined. Figure 4 reports F1, while Section 5.3 describes checking assigned document–theme pairs without explaining how recall, false negatives, or averaging are calculated. Annotation instructions, weighting across themes and sessions, and uncertainty estimates are missing. Treatment of unassigned documents also matters: Appendix B reports that up to 16.1% of LLM outputs are unlabeled. These gaps prevent a reliable interpretation of the system rankings.

Important reproducibility details remain unresolved despite the linked artifacts. As written, the design requires 36 synchronous participant slots, but reports 33 participants who each attended at most one synchronous experiment. A participant-to-session mapping is needed. The manuscript also omits the exact SBERT checkpoint and LLM decoding configuration. The interview component lacks a clear sample breakdown and qualitative analysis procedure.

Several explanations exceed the evidence. Two corpora with jointly varying domain, size, length, and semantic structure cannot establish their independent effects or the proposed cognitive mechanisms. Intervention richness is not experimentally isolated, and one 3B model supports limited conclusions about LLM systems generally. Reanalysis, clearer measurement definitions, and narrower claims are needed before the contribution meets the soundness threshold for Findings.
